text.p: Following are some of the main stories in Dutch newspapers today. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy. FINANCIEELE DAGBLAD
- Negotiations between bankrupt plane maker Fokker and South Korea's Samsung Aerospace enter "serious phase", says Dutch Economics Minister Hans Wijers. (p.1)
- Right-wing liberals VVD say Junior Finance Minister Wim Vermeend does not do enough to stop wealthy Dutch from emigrating to Belgium for lower tax reasons. (p.1)
- Dutch chemical industry association VNCI sees plastics recovery in second half of year on rising sales prices. (p.3)
- Publisher VNU and Rabobank join on the Internet. (p.3)
- Food and drinks group BolsWessanen and French Remy Cointreau merge Belgian distribution. (p.3)
- Builder Volker Stevin's in talks about taking over rail maintenance from Dutch Railways. (p.3)
- Fall in Dutch bankruptcies is slowing. (p.5) VOLKSKRANT

- Former Borsumij Wehry managers buy company clothes manufacturer EHCO-KLM from Borsumij's parent Hagemeijer at a considerably lower price than when Borsumij bought it in 1994. EHCO-KLM also pays them a super dividend, despite 1995 losses.
- Parliament divided over tackling greenhouse effect. (p.3)
- Northern province of Friesland floods former swamp. (p.9) DE TELEGRAAF
- Speeding fines for Dutch car drivers soar. Dutch also ignore red lights on massive scale. (p.1)
- Extra thick grass sods for damaged Ajax stadium pitch Arena. (p.1)
- Non-smokers' bonus at small Dutch company works, eight workers kicked the habit. (p.1)
- Injury-haunted Ajax win surprisingly from Auxerre. (p.1)
- Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm looks to transfer Stock Exchange's compliance and enforcement department to external watchdog body STE. (p.35) ALGEMEEN DAGBLAD
- Government wants to slow explosive growth of Schiphol airport for environmental reasons. (p.1)
- 36-hour working week no longer target for wage negotiations at union CNV, but larger rival FNV says trend for shorter working week continues. (p.11) TROUW
- Lower interest rates have led to lower mortgage payments, making the Dutch 1.5 billion guilders richer and the state 1.5 billion guilders poorer due to lost tax revenue.
